title: Move DIV/REM off the single-cycle ALU path
motivation:
The only recorded timing result has a very deep worst path running from the
pipeline registers through the forwarding muxes and into the execute ALU.
The current RV32M ALU implements DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU with single-cycle
SystemVerilog "/" and "%" operators, forcing Gowin timing to close a full
32-bit divider/remainder path in one cycle even though CoreMark's timed loop
is dominated by loads, stores, branches, simple integer ops, and MUL.

title: Split M-extension out of the EX ALU
motivation:
The current critical path is the forwarded EX operand path through the
monolithic ALU and back into the EX/MEM register. Because the ALU contains
combinational RV32M multiply and divide hardware in the same case tree as
ADD, branch compare, address generation, and CoreMark's hot integer ops,
every ordinary instruction pays for the longest arithmetic structure in
Fmax even when no M-extension instruction is executing.

title: Tiny BTB next-PC predictor
motivation:
The current five-stage core fetches the sequential PC until a branch or jump
resolves in EX, so every taken conditional branch and every jump pays a
front-end flush penalty. CoreMark's timed region has hot loops, direct calls,
and repeated returns, making taken-control penalties a plausible IPC loss that
can be attacked without touching the ALU critical path.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a small direct-mapped next-PC predictor in IF: a 16-entry BTB indexed by
fetch PC, with a modest tag, predicted target, and 2-bit taken counter. IF
uses a valid tag hit with a taken counter to fetch the predicted target;
otherwise it fetches PC+4. EX computes the architectural next PC exactly as
today, compares it with the predicted next PC carried down the pipe, and only
redirects/flushes on a mismatch. Update the BTB in EX for conditional
branches, JAL, and JALR; train conditional counters up/down and force jumps
strongly taken. This should remove most recurring loop and call/return
redirects while adding only a small PC-indexed lookup outside the current
forwarding-to-ALU worst path.

title: Remove redirect from fetch-decode mux
motivation:
After DIV/REM were moved out of the single-cycle ALU, the champion's
remaining worst path runs through the decode/front-end control loop rather
than through arithmetic: regfile/decode state feeds execute redirect, hazard
and fetch flushing, then returns to the ID/EX register input. The current
IF stage forces the combinational IF/ID instruction to NOP on redirect even
though ID already receives a redirect flush that bubbles the ID/EX register.
That redundant redirect-to-instruction mux makes the resolved branch signal
part of the decode, regfile-address, and load-use comparison path.

title: Register the IF/ID boundary
motivation:
The current champion's worst path no longer runs through the divider; it runs
from register-file state through ID/EX, EX redirect logic, the combinational
IF payload, hazard logic, and back into the ID/EX register. That loop exists
because if_stage emits a combinational IF/ID bundle and uses same-cycle
redirect/flush to rewrite the instruction to NOP before the hazard unit and
ID stage consume it. CoreMark now needs a structural timing cut in the
pipeline-control loop, not another arithmetic-unit change.

hypothesis.hypothesis:

enable, and kill behavior. Fetch should capture pc/instruction only when the

removed. The expected win is higher Fmax from a cleaner register-to-register
control boundary while preserving single-cycle MUL throughput and the current
single-retire RVFI contract.

title: Table-free backward branch predictor
motivation:
The existing core resolves every taken conditional branch in EX, so hot
CoreMark loops pay a front-end bubble on each taken back edge. A prior
16-entry BTB/counter predictor regressed badly because the table lookup and
predicted-PC plumbing inflated timing and area. The remaining predictor
opportunity is therefore a much cheaper static predictor that captures loop
behavior without any SRAM/LUTRAM state.

title: Share the single-cycle multiplier cone
motivation: The current champion keeps MUL on the single-cycle path, which prior runs show is important for CoreMark IPC, but alu.sv still builds three independent 64-bit multiplier products for MUL/MULH/MULHU/MULHSU on every ALU evaluation. title: Add a tiny instruction prefetch FIFO
motivation:
The current champion has already removed the divider from the hot execute
path and the remaining predictor-style front-end changes lost timing. The
benchmark still drives about 22% pseudo-random instruction-memory stalls,
and the current IF stage turns every one of those stalls into a front-end
bubble because it has no buffered instruction to feed decode. A small
sequential prefetch buffer is a structural way to recover IPC from those
stalls while leaving the proven EX/MUL datapath alone.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the purely combinational IF/ID feed with a two- or four-entry

sequential PC whenever the FIFO is not full, including during dmem/divider

and it preserves the existing RVFI order and trap behavior. The expected
win is higher CoreMark iterations/cycle by hiding isolated iStall cycles
behind already-buffered sequential instructions, with modest timing risk
because the FIFO control stays in the front end and avoids the EX ALU cone.

title: Tiny learned loop-target predictor
motivation:
The prior predictor attempts showed that CoreMark can benefit from fewer
taken-control bubbles, but the implementations lost too much Fmax by putting
BTB tables, IF-stage immediate decode, target adders, and predicted-next-PC
validation into already-sensitive control paths. The most promising remaining
predictor angle is to capture the same hot loop back-edges with far less
fetch logic.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a tiny exact-tag dynamic loop-target predictor that learns only real
taken backward conditional branches in EX. On each taken branch with a
negative immediate, update one or two registered entries containing the
branch PC and resolved target. In IF, prediction is only a PC-tag compare
against those entries and a mux from pc+4 to the stored target; there is no
instruction decode, B-immediate reconstruction, counter table, or target

existing architectural branch resolution and redirects on the two mismatch

predicted but actually taken redirects to the resolved target. This should
recover most repeated loop-backedge bubbles seen by the failed static
predictor while avoiding the long IF/EX plumbing that caused its Fmax loss.

title: Elide store-data load-use bubbles
motivation: The current champion has already removed the divider from the hot ALU path, and the recent predictor and prefetch attempts show that extra front-end control is expensive on this FPGA.  The remaining low-risk opportunity is IPC: the current load-use interlock stalls on any match against the following instruction's rs1 or rs2 fields, even when the consumer is a STORE whose rs2 data is not needed until MEM.  It can also stall on rs2 bit-fields for instructions that do not actually read rs2.

title: Exact early JAL target predictor
motivation:
The prior predictor attempts show that general branch target machinery is too expensive for this core: BTBs, backward-branch decode, and learned loop targets recovered some cycles but lengthened the fetch/control path enough to lose fitness. The remaining predictor opportunity should avoid tag tables, counters, branch-immediate decode for conditionals, and 32-bit predicted-target validation in EX.

Direct JAL instructions are different. They are architecturally always taken, their target is available from the fetched instruction bits, and suppressing their normal EX-stage redirect does not require a misprediction compare. CoreMark may use `JAL x0` for unconditional loop backedges and compiler control joins, plus ordinary calls; removing that one-cycle wrong-path fetch can improve IPC with much less timing risk than another dynamic branch predictor.

title: Posted store buffer for dmem stalls
motivation:
The accepted core now keeps single-cycle MUL throughput and has already split
the main execute result rails, so the remaining accepted structural wins are
harder to find on the pure ALU path.  The external benchmark injects roughly
22 percent random dmem backpressure, and the current hazard logic freezes the
entire pipeline for both loads and stores whenever a memory op in MEM sees
io_dmemReady low.  Stores have no register result for younger integer work to
consume, so stalling the whole pipe until the write bus accepts the store is
conservative but leaves CoreMark cycles on the table.

operand bypass mux is now part of the cycle-time limiter, not just the data

treats the prediction as an alias and repairs to pc+4 while flushing the
speculatively fetched target. This keeps target lookup local to IF and
carries only a small token to EX, while preserving correctness for symbolic
or changing instruction streams without the IF-side B-immediate fingerprint
cost that hurt the prior one-bit loop predictor. Do not predict JALR or

read path as a simple x0-or-array mux. When the predictor is wrong, detected
by comparing IF/ID rs1/rs2 against the WB rd/control bits, insert one decode
bubble and hold fetch so the consumer rereads the just-written architectural
value on the next cycle.

This moves the rare WB-to-ID dependency from a 32-bit data mux on every ID
operand into a small control interlock. It avoids the IF next-PC predictor
costs that have repeatedly regressed, should shorten ID/EX setup and
writeback-to-decode timing, and preserves exact RVFI/register semantics by
stalling rather than executing with a stale operand.
